explain.say: Concrete looks eternal, yet seafront buildings and bridges from Mumbai to Miami crumble at their edges after a few decades. The culprit is usually not the concrete but the steel inside, quietly rusting. On the board, follow the slow march of carbon dioxide and salt from the air towards the bar.

explain.say: Fresh concrete is strongly alkaline, around pH thirteen, and that wraps the steel in a thin protective film. The cover concrete is the guard. Carbon dioxide from the air slowly reacts with it, which is called carbonation, and lowers the pH. When the carbonated zone reaches the steel, the film is lost. What do you think happens next?

explain.say: Before that, how fast does it creep in? Carbonation grows with the square root of time. At a typical rate of four millimetres per root year, it reaches twenty millimetres in twenty five years, but takes a hundred years to reach forty. So doubling the cover can make it last four times as long. That is why cover is precious.

Once protection is lost, the steel rusts. Rust takes up several times the volume of the steel it came from, so it swells and pushes the cover off, first as cracks along the bar, then as chunks falling away, called spalling. Sea salts, chlorides, are even worse: they break the film without any carbonation.

explain.say: So durable design means enough cover for the exposure, a low water–cement ratio for dense concrete, good curing, and cracks kept narrow, usually under about zero point three millimetres. IS 456 asks for twenty to seventy five millimetres of cover depending on exposure. Brilliant! Challenge: why does a pier in the sea need more cover than a beam indoors?

faq.a: Carbonation is the slow reaction of carbon dioxide from the air with the alkaline compounds in concrete. It lowers the pH from about 13 to below about 9, removing the protection around the steel.

faq.q: Why does steel in concrete rust?
faq.a: Steel is protected by a thin film that forms in alkaline concrete. When carbonation or chlorides reach the bar, the film breaks down and, with water and oxygen, the steel corrodes.

Cover is the barrier between the steel and the weather. Since carbonation depth grows with the square root of time, a little extra cover buys many extra years of life, and it also protects against fire.
asks: How much cover does rebar need?

faq.a: Spalling is when pieces of concrete break off the surface, usually because rusting steel underneath has swelled and pushed the cover away.
Chloride ions from seawater or de-icing salts travel through the cover and break down the protective film on the steel, even when the concrete is still alkaline, causing fast, pitting corrosion.

facts: Rust can occupy roughly two to six times the volume of the iron it forms from.
IS 456 sets nominal cover from 20 mm for mild exposure to 75 mm for extreme exposure.
Carbonation depth grows roughly with the square root of time.
